title: Leveling the Playing Field -- Ch. 18: Sanlakas v. Executive Secretary: Constitutionality of a "State of Rebellion"
keywords: capable of repetition yet evading review
Integrated Bar of the Philippines v. Zamora
primary_topics: Chapter 18 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' -- CJP's account of Sanlakas v. Executive Secretary, the consolidated Petitions challenging President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo's Proclamation No. 427 and General Order No. 4 declaring a state of rebellion after the July 27, 2003 Oakwood incident

The Tinga ponencia's doctrine that Section 18 of Article VII grants the President 'a sequence of graduated powers,' that the calling out power requires no conditions, and that a declaration of a state of rebellion is 'an utter superfluity' that is 'deemed not written'

CJP's own Separate Opinion, joined by Justices Quisumbing and Callejo, arguing that the Petitions should have been dismissed solely on the ground of mootness -- and that 'capable of repetition yet evading review' may be invoked only where the Court has jurisdiction over the subject matter

His epilogue tallying the fractured vote (11-2 dismissal but only five justices expressly upholding constitutionality) to show that, contrary to the ponente's wish, the constitutional question had not been laid to rest
sub_topics: The precedent: the May 1, 2001 'EDSA 3' mob assault on Malacañang led GMA to declare a state of rebellion through Proclamation No. 38 and General Order No. 1, which she lifted five days later, mooting Lacson v. Perez

The facts: on July 27, 2003 some 300 AFP officers and enlisted men stormed the Oakwood Premiere Apartments in Makati demanding the resignation of the President, the defense secretary and the PNP chief, prompting Proclamation No. 427 and General Order No. 4
The mutiny ended that same evening, but the state of rebellion was lifted only on August 1, 2003 through Proclamation No. 435; in the interim four Petitions were filed and consolidated

Justice Tinga agreed with the Solicitor General that the cases were moot, yet wrote on the merits because the question was 'capable of repetition yet evading review' and urged the Court to lay the issue to rest

The ruling: the graduated Commander-in-Chief powers -- calling out, suspension of the writ, martial law -- with only the latter two requiring actual invasion or rebellion plus the demands of public safety, as Integrated Bar of the Philippines v. Zamora had observed

The ponencia traced the powers to the US Constitution and invoked Marcos v. Manglapus on the President's 'unstated residual powers,' concluding that the authority to declare a state of rebellion sprang from executive power reinforced by commander-in-chief power
The holding that such a declaration is 'an utter superfluity,' 'devoid of any legal significance' and 'deemed not written,' and that it does not diminish constitutionally protected rights
Justice Vitug's two-page Separate Opinion, 'in complete agreement' but emphasizing that the proclamation cannot countenance acts violative of fundamental rights

CJP's Separate Opinion: the lifting of the issuances left no extant proclamation or order to declare valid or void, the case had become a plea for declaratory relief beyond the Court's original jurisdiction, and the petitioners showed no direct and continuing prejudice

His limiting principle: the 'capable of repetition yet evading review' theory may be invoked only when the Supreme Court has jurisdiction over the subject matter -- as in an appealed judgment, not an original action for declaratory relief

Justice Ynares-Santiago's Separate Opinion voting to grant: the issuances were null and void for grave abuse of discretion and had served as legal cover for warrantless arrests, citing the arrest of Ramon Cardenas and the linking of Senators Honasan and Loi Ejercito and Mayor JV Ejercito

Justice SandovalGutierrez's Separate Opinion: no constitutional provision authorizes a declaration of a state of rebellion, extra-constitutional measures are unnecessary where the law provides for emergencies, and the US cases cited were inapposite

The epilogue's vote count: only Tinga, Vitug, Carpio, Corona and Morales voted expressly for constitutionality; Davide, Puno and Martinez concurred only in the result; Quisumbing and Callejo joined CJP on mootness; Santiago and Gutierrez dissented; Azcuna was on leave and one seat was vacant

stances.claim: The Petitions should have been dismissed on the sole ground of mootness, because the President's own lifting of the issuances left no extant proclamation or order that could be declared valid or void, and what remained was a plea for declaratory relief over which the Supreme Court has no original jurisdiction.
stances.rhetorical_move: procedural minimalism: refusing to reach a constitutional question once the live controversy has disappeared

stances.claim: The theory that a question is 'capable of repetition yet evading review' may be invoked only when the Supreme Court has jurisdiction over the subject matter and the party raising it was, or continued to be, directly and pecuniarily prejudiced -- conditions the petitioners here did not meet.
stances.rhetorical_move: narrowing an exception by attaching jurisdictional and injury preconditions, and contrasting an original action with an appealed judgment

stances.claim: Despite the 11-2 dismissal, the Court did not definitively uphold the constitutionality of a presidential declaration of a state of rebellion, since only five justices voted expressly in its favor while others concurred only in the result, dissented, or voted on mootness alone.
stances.rhetorical_move: vote-counting audit of the decision, weighing each separate opinion to measure what was actually settled

notable_anecdotes: CJP recounts writing his own Separate Opinion in the case, joined by Justices Quisumbing and Callejo, urging that the Petitions be dismissed for mootness alone rather than on the constitutional merits.

He recalls the Oakwood incident itself: in the wee hours of July 27, 2003 some three hundred AFP officers and enlisted men stormed an apartment complex in Makati's financial center demanding the resignation of the President, the defense secretary and the PNP chief.

He notes the odd sequence that troubled Justice Ynares-Santiago -- the soldiers returned to barracks by the evening of July 27, yet the state of rebellion stayed in force until August 1, a window in which Ramon Cardenas was arrested and presented to media in handcuffs.

In the epilogue he personally tallies the justices one by one -- five for constitutionality, three concurring only in the result, three on mootness, two dissenting, one on leave and one vacancy -- to show that the ponente's wish to lay the issue to rest went unfulfilled.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 18 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' recounted Sanlakas v. Executive Secretary, the four consolidated Petitions that challenged President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo's Proclamation No. 427 and General Order No. 4, which declared a state of rebellion and called out the Armed Forces after some three hundred officers and enlisted men seized the Oakwood Premiere Apartments in Makati on July 27, 2003. CJP first recalled the precedent of the May 1, 2001 'EDSA 3' assault on Malacañang, where a similar declaration was lifted after five days and the challenge in Lacson v. Perez was dismissed as moot. Here the mutiny ended the same evening but the state of rebellion stood until August 1, 2003. Justice Dante O. Tinga, though agreeing the cases were moot, wrote on the merits because the question was 'capable of repetition yet evading review.' His ponencia held that Section 18 of Article VII grants the President 'a sequence of graduated powers,' that the conditions of actual invasion or rebellion and the demands of public safety attach only to the suspension of the writ and to martial law, and that the President's executive power, reinforced by the 'unstated residual powers' recognized in Marcos v. Manglapus, supported the declaration -- which was in any case 'an utter superfluity,' 'devoid of any legal significance' and 'deemed not written.' CJP, joined by Justices Quisumbing and Callejo, wrote separately to argue that the Petitions should be dismissed on mootness alone: nothing extant remained to be declared valid or void, the suits had become pleas for declaratory relief outside the Court's original jurisdiction, and the repetition theory may be invoked only where the Court has jurisdiction over the subject matter and the party remains directly prejudiced. He summarized Justice Vitug's concurrence, and the Santiago and Gutierrez opinions voting to grant the Petitions, then tallied the votes to conclude that, with only five justices expressly upholding constitutionality, the question had not been definitively laid to rest.
